elements.element: Vendor may audit no more than once in any 12-month period.
elements.evidence: The inserted sentence caps investigations at "no more than once per year," which on a literal reading permits a calendar-year rather than rolling 12-month limit (two investigations could straddle a year boundary within 12 months). To meet the preferred element the drafter must say "no more than once in any twelve (12) month period."

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 30 days' written notice of an audit.
elements.evidence: Rendered text gives "at least fifteen (15) days' notice" and does not require it to be in writing; 30 days' written notice is absent.
No timing restriction appears anywhere in 11.3 as rendered; the insertion addresses frequency, notice and cost only.

elements.element: Audits are conducted by an independent auditor.
elements.evidence: The clause leaves the investigation with IBM itself ("IBM may investigate potential violations"); no independent auditor is required.

elements.element: The auditor is bound by confidentiality obligations.
elements.evidence: No auditor is designated and no confidentiality undertaking for any investigator is inserted.

elements.element: Audits are conducted off-site where possible.
elements.evidence: No off-site preference language appears in the rendered clause.

elements.element: Vendor bears audit costs unless underpayment exceeds 5 percent.
elements.evidence: Cost shifting threshold is set at "underpayment by Customer exceeding ten percent (10%)", not 5 percent.

elements.element: Vendor has no direct access to Customer systems for an audit.
elements.evidence: No prohibition on direct access to Customer systems was inserted, and 11.3 retains an unqualified right to "investigate potential violations" without any access carve-out.

elements.element: Vendor may audit no more than once per year.
elements.evidence: Inserted: "IBM may investigate potential violations under this Subsection 11.3 no more than once per year" — an express annual frequency cap binding the sole Customer-facing verification right.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 15 days' notice of an audit.
elements.evidence: Inserted: "and only after giving Customer at least fifteen (15) days' notice." The fallback does not require the notice to be written, and the emergency carve-out in the retained paragraph is expressly limited to notification before Subsection 11.3(a)/(b) activities, so it does not erode this investigation-notice condition.

elements.element: Vendor bears audit costs unless underpayment exceeds 10 percent.
elements.evidence: Inserted: "IBM will bear all costs of any such investigation unless it reveals an underpayment by Customer exceeding ten percent (10%)." Default cost sits with Vendor and the shift trigger matches the 10% threshold; the trigger is self-contained (an underpayment revealed by the investigation) and not undefined.

reasons: Fallback checklist is complete: the single inserted sentence pair supplies the annual frequency cap, the 15-day notice condition and the 10% cost-shifting threshold in operative language, not merely in the margin comment.

Preferred level is not reached: 30 days' written notice, business hours, independent auditor, auditor confidentiality, off-site conduct, the 5% threshold and the no-system-access prohibition are all absent. Note also that "once per year" is weaker than "once in any 12-month period" if the preferred position is later pursued.

Minimal: nothing outside the three fallback parameters was added or deleted; the existing warranty-investigation right, IBM's 11.3(a)/(b) remedies and the emergency notification carve-out are all retained verbatim, and no survival tail, expense language or procedure was bolted on.

Preserves intent: the insertion attaches conditions to the investigation right only; IBM's remedial actions under 11.3(a)/(b) and the emergency/legal-requirement exception to pre-action notification continue to operate, and no cross-reference or defined term is left dangling.

Optional hardening (not required at fallback): if the counterparty pushes back on a 15-day wait before investigating suspected AUP breaches, consider carving out investigations conducted in an emergency while keeping the cost allocation intact, rather than conceding the frequency cap.
